prompt: What does a static analysis tool do with the code it is given?

choices.text: Runs it in a sandbox and watches what it does
choices.why: That is closer to dynamic analysis; static analysis never runs the program.

choices.text: Matches it against rules somebody wrote, without running it
choices.why: Right. It finds the shapes it has rules for, and nothing else.

choices.text: Compares it with a database of published security advisories
choices.why: That is composition analysis of dependencies, lesson 5.

choices.text: Proves that it has no vulnerabilities left
choices.why: A clean run says no rule that ran found its shape; it proves nothing about the rest.

prompt: Match each part of linkbox's search to its role in the flow a security rule looks for.

pairs.right: a source: data somebody outside controls
a sink: a call that runs what it is given as SQL
the path: data formatted into the code
the fix: the value passed as a parameter

right_distractors: a header the browser adds to the response

prompt: Which of these can static analysis of linkbox's source not see? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A security header missing from the HTTP response
choices.why: Right: a property of the answer at runtime, which is lesson 4's dynamic analysis.

choices.text: A flaw inside Flask itself
choices.why: Right: it is in a dependency, which is lesson 5.

choices.text: An environment variable that turns debugging on in production
choices.why: Right: configuration is outside the code that was scanned.

choices.text: A query built by formatting the search text into SQL
choices.why: This is exactly the shape Bandit's B608 and the project's Semgrep rule match.

prompt: Bandit's first run on ~/linkbox, with the .venv inside it, reported 436 findings. How many of them were in the project's own files?
Why does the lesson call a first run with hundreds of findings in .venv the most damaging one?

choices.text: Because those findings are all false positives
choices.why: Many may be real in their own context; the damage is to how the tool is seen.

choices.text: The developer decides the tool is noise, for good
choices.why: Right. The first thing to tune is what the tool reads.

choices.text: Because scanning .venv takes longer than the push budget
choices.why: The scan was quick; the cost the lesson names is trust.

choices.text: Because Bandit cannot scan installed packages correctly
choices.why: It scanned them the same way as the project; it was simply pointed at code that is not yours.

prompt: B608 on the search was reported with medium confidence. What does that score describe?

choices.text: How harmful the injection would be if it is real
choices.why: That is severity, the other score.

choices.text: How sure the check is that the case is real
choices.why: Right. Bandit cannot see what q holds, so it is not certain.

choices.text: How often the rule is wrong across all Python projects
choices.why: It is a judgement about this finding, not a statistic about the rule.

choices.text: How likely an attacker is to find the flaw
choices.why: Bandit says nothing about attackers; it scores its own evidence.

prompt: Bandit flags `assert user.is_admin` in a route with low severity and high confidence. A colleague says low severity means it can wait. What does the lesson's reading of the two scores suggest?

choices.text: Agree: severity is the score that decides urgency
choices.why: In a test that would be fair; in a route the assert is the access check, and -O removes it.

choices.text: Disagree: high confidence means it must be fixed first
choices.why: Confidence is about the evidence, not urgency; the reason to act is what the assert guards.

choices.text: Look at the line: here it is the access check
choices.why: Right. The scores describe the rule's view; the context says this one is a real defect.

choices.text: Skip B101 everywhere, since it fires on tests
choices.why: That is the move the lesson rejects: it would hide exactly this line.

prompt: Bandit does not report that create() compares the token with !=. What is that, in the lesson's vocabulary?

choices.text: A true negative
choices.why: A true negative is a correct silence; this silence is about a real defect.

choices.text: A false positive
choices.why: A false positive is a report; here there is no report at all.

choices.text: A false negative
choices.why: Right: a real defect the tool did not report, the expensive kind.

choices.text: A true positive
choices.why: A true positive is a report about a real defect, like B608 on the search.

prompt: Six B101 findings sit on the asserts in tests/test_app.py. Why does bandit.yaml skip B101 for the tests only, instead of everywhere?

choices.text: Because skipping a rule everywhere needs administrator rights on the machine
choices.why: It is one line of configuration; the reason is what the rule still catches elsewhere.

choices.text: Because an assert in application code is a real defect under -O
choices.why: Right. Skipping it everywhere would turn that into a false negative.

choices.text: Because the tests directory is excluded from the scan anyway
choices.why: Only .venv is excluded; the tests are scanned, which is why B101 fired there.

choices.text: Because pytest removes its asserts when run under -O
choices.why: pytest rewrites asserts to report them; the point is nobody runs tests under -O.

prompt: A comment reads `# nosec B608: t is one of TABLES`. What did Bandit do with it in the lesson?

choices.text: Ignored the whole comment and reported B608 anyway
choices.why: The finding was suppressed and the exit status was 0.

choices.text: Suppressed B608 and stored the reason in its report for reviewers
choices.why: Bandit has no field for a reason; it read the words as check ids.

choices.text: Refused the file as a syntax error
choices.why: It parsed the file fine and only warned.

choices.text: Suppressed it, warning once per word as an unknown id
choices.why: Right. The reason belongs on the line above, with the ids alone after nosec.

prompt: In bandit.yaml, the setting that keeps the virtual environment out of every scan is called ___.
create() checks the token inline, and the rule writes-need-the-token flags it. What is the finding, in the lesson's terms?

choices.text: A false positive, since the route rejects a missing token
choices.why: The rule did not say the route is open; it said the route does not call require_token(), which was true.

choices.text: A true positive of the rule, which enforces one checking function
choices.why: Right. Whether the rule is right to want the call is the question it raises.

choices.text: A false negative of Bandit that Semgrep corrected
choices.why: Semgrep reported it, so for Semgrep it is a positive; Bandit's silence is a separate matter.

choices.text: A true negative, because lesson 1's test passes
choices.why: A finding was reported, so it cannot be a negative.

prompt: Why does the lesson prefer secrets.compare_digest() to != for the token?

choices.text: Because != fails on tokens longer than 32 characters
choices.why: != compares strings of any length; the issue is how long it takes.

choices.text: Because compare_digest() also hashes the token
choices.why: It stores nothing; it only compares.

choices.text: Because != stops at the first difference, and its timing leaks
choices.why: Right: how long it takes says how much of a guess is right. compare_digest() takes the same time whatever the input.

choices.text: Because Bandit's B105 requires it
choices.why: B105 is about the token being written in the code; it says nothing about comparison.

prompt: Which call does the rule sql-built-from-a-string not match?

choices.text: db().execute("SELECT url FROM links WHERE code = ?", (code,))
choices.why: Right: a plain string and a tuple of parameters, like follow().

choices.text: db().execute("SELECT url FROM links WHERE code = '" + code + "'")
choices.why: A string joined with + is one of the four patterns.

choices.text: db().execute("SELECT url FROM links WHERE code = '{}'".format(code))
choices.why: .format() is one of the four patterns.

choices.text: db().execute(f"SELECT url FROM links WHERE code = '{code}'")
choices.why: An f-string is the first pattern of the rule.

prompt: What happens if ci/sast.sh calls semgrep without --error and Semgrep finds the SQL rule's shape?

choices.text: It prints the finding and the stage passes
choices.why: Right. Without --error Semgrep exits 0, and the pipeline looks like it checked something.

choices.text: Semgrep refuses to start without an exit policy
choices.why: It runs and reports; only the exit status changes.

choices.text: Bandit's exit status breaks the build instead
choices.why: Bandit only fails on its own findings; it knows nothing of Semgrep's.

choices.text: The stage fails with a warning that is counted
choices.why: There is no warning status in this pipeline yet; lesson 7 adds one.

prompt: B105, the token in settings.py, is a true positive, yet ci/sast.sh does not break on it. What reason does the lesson give?

choices.text: Low-severity findings are false by definition
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite: B105 is true.

choices.text: Its confidence is only medium
choices.why: B608 has medium confidence too and does break the build; the stage filters on severity.

choices.text: Its fix is not a code change, so no push clears it
choices.why: Right: breaking on it would block every push for work nobody does in their change. Lesson 6 is about it, and lesson 7 generalises the rule.

choices.text: Semgrep already reports it in the same stage, so Bandit need not
choices.why: Neither of the project's two Semgrep rules is about secrets.

prompt: Put the stages of ci/stages, as this lesson leaves it, in the order they run.
What did the new test show before the fix, when it searched for it's?

choices.text: A 500 from the search, because SQLite refused the query
choices.why: Right: near "s": syntax error, and Flask answered 500.

choices.text: An empty page, because nothing matched
choices.why: The page never rendered; the query failed first.

choices.text: A 401, because the test sent no token
choices.why: The search needs no token; the link was created with one.

choices.text: Every link in the database
choices.why: That is what an empty search returns; this one failed.

prompt: Why does the lesson write the failing test before changing the query?

choices.text: Because Bandit only stops reporting B608 once a test exists
choices.why: Bandit reads the code's shape and knows nothing about tests.

choices.text: To prove the test catches the defect, in any form
choices.why: Right. A silent scanner says the shape is gone, not that the behaviour is right.

choices.text: Because the pipeline runs tests before static analysis
choices.why: The order of stages is not why; the test's value is in failing first.

choices.text: Because pytest refuses a test that passes on its first run
choices.why: pytest has no such rule.

prompt: linkbox's image starts gunicorn, so app.run(debug=True) never ran in it. Why remove it anyway?

choices.text: Because gunicorn refuses to load a file that contains it
choices.why: gunicorn imports app and ignores the block; it never refused.

choices.text: Because it slows down every request
choices.why: It does nothing under gunicorn, which is the point: it is dead code until somebody runs the file.

choices.text: It becomes live if somebody runs python app.py
choices.why: Right. The debugger would then run typed Python for whoever reaches the page.

choices.text: Because Semgrep's writes-need-the-token rule flags it
choices.why: That rule is about POST routes; Bandit's B201 is the one that flagged the debugger.

prompt: A teammate proposes adding `skips: [B608]` to bandit.yaml because the table-name query in a report script is a false positive. What would the lesson have them do?

choices.text: Accept it: one false positive justifies switching off the check
choices.why: Switching it off everywhere hides the next real injection, the false negative the lesson warns about.

choices.text: Raise the stage's threshold to high severity
choices.why: That would let the search's B608 through as well.

choices.text: A `# nosec B608` on that one line, with the reason on the line above
choices.why: Right. One line, the check named, a reason a reviewer checks.

choices.text: Exclude the report script's directory from Bandit
choices.why: A directory exclusion is a wider hole than the one line that is wrong.

prompt: Somebody adds a route `@app.post("/links/<code>/delete")` that deletes a link and forgets require_token(). With the pipeline as this lesson leaves it, what stops the push?

choices.text: Bandit, because deleting without a check is a known Python pattern
choices.why: None of Bandit's built-in checks knows linkbox's token convention.

choices.text: The tests, because lesson 1's token test covers every route
choices.why: That test posts to /links only; nobody wrote one for the new route.

choices.text: Nothing until the dynamic scan of lesson 4
choices.why: The static analysis stage already has a rule for exactly this shape.

choices.text: The sast stage, through Semgrep's writes-need-the-token
choices.why: Right. A POST route that never calls require_token() is the shape the project's own rule matches.
